why: Both moved the same single call the same way with behaviour intact, so the decision rests on the system read: B's improvements are the ones specific to THIS app (catalog-driven vision instead of a wrong substring list, per-message client churn, Router-only fields shipped in the migration itself) and it reasons explicitly about what it declines, while A's four are mostly the generic Router plays plus one — cross-vendor fallbacks — that is arguably the wrong default for a Discord bot. A is the better-evidenced report (far more live traffic through the real on_message path, a 3×3 model comparison rather than one question) and its measured tier=flex under a models list casts doubt on B's reason for skipping fallbacks, which is why the margin is slight rather than clear.
A_best: Evidence depth: 14 live on_message calls in the outside check, the cache win measured end to end on the app's own prompt shape ($0.0148 → $0.0045), and the cheap-default argued from three prompts × three configurations with answers compared, not one sample.
B_best: System-level judgment that goes past the standard Router levers — deriving image support from Router's catalog (fixes /model in both directions: gpt-6-luna gains vision, text-only gpt-4 stops being sent images), reusing clients per provider, and declining fallbacks with a stated Flex tradeoff rather than shipping them reflexively.
A_worst: Shipping cross-vendor fallbacks as a policy default for a hobby chat bot while claiming they cost nothing, against B's measurement that a models list disables Flex; the candidate list is also hardcoded, and i2/i3 both write router.policy.json so the two branches must be hand-merged.
B_worst: Its own validation records just one live on_message request (the rest are probe features), so the report's confident live claims — Flex candidates, the corrupt-image fallback, the policy on all 16 calls — rest on side probes rather than the bot's path, and the model swap is argued from a single question.
